q: Docker Compose runs 3 copies of your API on one server, and the server loses power. What happens to the copies?
options: Compose starts them again on another server
All 3 stop, because Compose only manages the machine it runs on
Two stop and one keeps running
Nothing, containers do not need a server
why: Compose looks after containers on one machine and does not know that other machines exist. Kubernetes treats many machines as one group, so it can start the pods on a machine that is still alive.

q: A Deployment says replicas: 3. Someone deletes one of the 3 pods by hand. What happens, and who types a command?
options: Nothing happens until you run kubectl apply again
The same pod is repaired and keeps its name
A loop sees 2 pods where 3 are wanted and creates a new pod with a new name, and nobody types a command
The Service creates a new pod
why: You write what you want, and a loop (the ReplicaSet) compares what you want with what exists, again and again. It counts 2, wants 3, and creates one. The new pod is a new pod, not the old one brought back.

q: A pod dies and a new pod takes its place. Which statement is true?
options: The new pod has the same name and the same IP address
The new pod has a new name and a new IP address, so you should call a Service and not a pod
The new pod has the same IP address but a new name
You must change the config to use the new IP address
why: A pod is disposable: it is replaced, not repaired. Because the address changes, other parts of the system call a Service, which keeps one stable name and IP.

q: You change the image tag in a Deployment from 1.4.0 to 1.5.0 and apply it. What does Kubernetes do?
options: It changes the image inside the running containers
It makes a new ReplicaSet and moves the pods over a few at a time
It stops everything and then starts the new version
Nothing, you must delete the old pods by hand
why: A change to the pod blueprint starts a rolling update: the Deployment makes a new ReplicaSet, scales it up and scales the old one down. The old ReplicaSet is kept, which makes a rollback with kubectl rollout undo possible.

q: A Service has the selector app=shop-api. Which pods get its traffic?
options: Every pod in the cluster
Pods whose labels match app=shop-api, even when they are not ready
Pods whose labels match app=shop-api and that are ready
Only the oldest pod
why: A pod needs both: the label matches, and it is ready. A pod that fails its readiness check is left out until it is ready again, and a selector that matches no label gives an empty list.

q: You apply an Ingress to a new cluster that has no ingress controller. What happens to the requests?
options: They are routed by the rules anyway
Nothing: an Ingress is only rules, and a controller must read them
Kubernetes installs a controller for you
The Deployment restarts
why: The Kubernetes docs say: only creating an Ingress resource has no effect. You must run an ingress controller. For new work the project recommends Gateway API, because the Ingress API is frozen.
